scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a claim response that largely accepts well-being as the measure of leadership while noting other measures; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: We naturally judge leaders by what their leadership actually does for ordinary people.
Some people claim that the effectiveness of a country's leaders is best measured by the well-being of its citizens.
I largely agree with this claim, though I believe a few other measures of leadership also matter.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why well-being is the key measure

sentences.text: First, the well-being of citizens is indeed the clearest sign of effective leadership.
Leaders exist to serve their people, so the condition of those people reveals how well they have led.
For example, a government that improves health, safety, and jobs has plainly done its work well.
This shows that the lives of ordinary people are a fair and direct test of leadership.
Grand speeches mean little if the people of a nation continue to suffer.
Judging leaders by results keeps them focused on the needs of those they serve.
For these reasons, citizens' well-being is a powerful measure of effective leadership.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why other measures matter too

sentences.text: Second, however, well-being alone does not capture everything about effective leadership.
Some leaders inherit disasters and improve them slowly, even while their people still struggle.
Consider a leader who guides a nation wisely through a war whose hardships no one could have avoided.
Such cases show that short-term well-being can be an unfair measure of a leader's true skill.
Effective leadership also includes protecting freedom, justice, and the long-term future of a nation.
A leader who raises living standards by crushing all liberty has not truly led well.
Well-being, then, is the best single measure but not the only one.
In conclusion, the well-being of citizens is the strongest measure of a leader's effectiveness.
But it must be weighed alongside justice, freedom, and the challenges a leader inherits.
We judge leaders best by how well their people live, while remembering all that good leadership requires.
